summary: Eight of the nine steps teach rules that show up as return values and object state (branch order, loop mutation, defaults, sort keys, classes, super(), iterators, closures); Arrays and lists teaches what a list is underneath and what it costs, which no check can see.

steps.title: Branching with if, elif and else
steps.reason: A branch chain shows up as the label a function returns, and the page names three mistakes a check catches: the looser test placed first, a truthiness guard that lumps 0 with None, and a missing guard for None. The task labels a ticket's age so it stays off the exercise's four-way status function.

steps.title: Loops: while for a condition, for over a collection
steps.reason: Removing items from a list while a for loop walks it leaves the list in a state a check can see, and the page shows the skipped duplicate. The while re-ask loop is ruled out because it needs input(), which meets end-of-file in the page.

steps.title: Functions: naming a rule once
steps.reason: The mutable default argument and the missing return both show up in what two calls return. A sibling of the page's add_note, on tags, keeps the page's example from being the answer.

steps.title: Lambda and sort keys
steps.reason: A sort key shows up as the order of the returned list, and the page names the alphabetical-text key, the missing tie-breaker and sorting the caller's list in place. The exercise sorts by priority rank, so the task sorts by status rank instead.

steps.title: Arrays and lists
steps.reason: The step teaches what a list is underneath, what array.array saves and what insert(0) and pop(0) cost; none of that is behaviour a check can tell apart. Its one behavioural trap, the shallow copy, needs a deep-copy idiom the page does not teach.

steps.title: OOP concepts, classes and objects
steps.reason: A small class shows up as instance state, method return values and its __repr__ text, and the page names a missing __repr__ and printing instead of returning. The task builds an Agent so it stays off the exercise's Ticket.

steps.title: Inheritance: one rule overridden
steps.reason: An override and a subclass __init__ show up as attributes and return values, and the page names the forgotten super().__init__ and the override that drops the parent's rule. The base class fits in the starter, and the override is a label, not the exercise's halved deadline.

steps.title: Iterators: what a for loop does underneath
steps.reason: iter() and next() on a plain iterable show up in what a function returns, and the page names the two mistakes a check catches: indexing something that is only an iterator, and asking a list for a second, fresh iterator. A class with __iter__ and __len__ is left alone because it is the exercise's Desk.

steps.title: Scope: where a name is looked up
steps.reason: A closure counter shows up in what successive calls return, and the page names the UnboundLocalError from a missing nonlocal and the shared state of a global. The exercise's counter is the class attribute Desk.next_id, so a closure stays off it.

tasks.title: Branching
tasks.idea: The reader writes age_label(hours_open), where hours_open is a number or None when the opening time is unknown. It returns "unknown" for None, "stale" from 72 hours, "aging" from 24 hours and "fresh" below that, so age_label(30) is "aging" and age_label(0) is "fresh".
checks: 80 hours gives "stale", which fails a chain that tests the 24-hour bound first.
30 hours gives "aging".
0 hours gives "fresh", which fails a guard written as `if not hours_open`.
None gives "unknown", which fails a chain with no guard for None.
tasks.q: Write age_label(hours_open). hours_open is how long a ticket has been open, in hours, or None when its opening time is unknown. Return "unknown" for None, "stale" from 72 hours up, "aging" from 24 hours up, and "fresh" below 24. So age_label(30) is "aging" and age_label(0) is "fresh".
tasks.tests:
assert age_label(72) == "stale", "72 hours is already stale"
assert age_label(24) == "aging", "24 hours is already aging"
assert age_label(0) == "fresh", "0 hours is fresh, not unknown"
assert age_label(None) == "unknown", "None is unknown"

tasks.title: Loops
tasks.idea: The reader writes drop_ids(ids, closed): it removes from the list ids, in place, every id that is in closed, and keeps the rest in their order. With ids = [101, 102, 102, 103] and closed = {102}, ids ends up as [101, 103].
checks: Two equal ids next to each other are both removed, which fails ids.remove() inside a for loop over ids.
The ids that stay keep their original order.
The caller's list object is the one that changes, which fails a body that only rebinds the local name ids to a new list.
tasks.q: Write drop_ids(ids, closed). It removes from the list ids every id that is in closed, and the ids that stay keep their order. Change the caller's list itself; the function does not need to return anything. With ids = [101, 102, 102, 103], calling drop_ids(ids, {102}) leaves ids as [101, 103].
tasks.tests:
pair = [101, 102, 102, 103]
drop_ids(pair, {102})
assert pair == [101, 103], "removes two equal ids that sit next to each other"
mixed = [105, 101, 104, 103]
drop_ids(mixed, {101})
assert mixed == [105, 104, 103], "keeps the other ids in their order"
queue = [201, 202, 203]
drop_ids(queue, {202})
assert queue == [201, 203], "changes the caller's list, not a copy of it"

tasks.title: Functions
tasks.idea: The reader writes add_tag(tag, tags=None): it appends tag to tags and returns the list, starting a new list when no tags are passed. add_tag("printer") returns ["printer"], and a second add_tag("vpn") returns ["vpn"].
checks: A second call without tags returns a list holding only its own tag, which fails a tags=[] default.
Passing a list appends to that list and returns it.
The function returns the list, which fails a body that prints it and returns None.
tasks.q: Write add_tag(tag, tags), where callers may leave tags out, so give it a default. The function appends tag to the list tags and returns that list; when no list is passed, it starts a new one. So add_tag("printer") returns ["printer"], and a second call, add_tag("vpn"), returns ["vpn"].
tasks.tests:
add_tag("printer")
assert add_tag("vpn") == ["vpn"], "a second call without a list starts a list of its own"
mine = []
result = add_tag("printer", mine)
assert result is mine and mine == ["printer"], "appends to the list you pass and returns that list"
assert add_tag("lan", ["vpn"]) == ["vpn", "lan"], "returns the list with the new tag at the end"

tasks.title: Lambda and sort keys
tasks.idea: The reader writes by_status(tickets) for ticket dicts with "id" and "status" keys, using STATUS_RANK = {"breached": 1, "at risk": 2, "on time": 3}. It returns a new list sorted by that rank, ties broken by id, so breached tickets come first.
checks: A breached ticket comes before an at-risk one, which fails a key on the status text ("at risk" sorts first alphabetically).
Two tickets with the same status come out in id order, which fails a key without the tie-breaker when they start out of order.
The caller's list keeps its order, which fails tickets.sort().
tasks.q: Each ticket is a dict with "id" and "status" keys, and STATUS_RANK in the starter gives each status a rank. Write by_status(tickets). It returns a new list of the tickets sorted by that rank, so breached tickets come first, then at-risk ones, then on-time ones, and tickets with the same status come out in id order. The caller's list keeps its own order. For [{"id": 2, "status": "on time"}, {"id": 1, "status": "breached"}] it returns ticket 1 first, then ticket 2.
tasks.tests:
mixed = [{"id": 1, "status": "at risk"}, {"id": 2, "status": "breached"}]
assert [t["id"] for t in by_status(mixed)] == [2, 1], "a breached ticket comes before an at-risk one"
same = [{"id": 9, "status": "on time"}, {"id": 4, "status": "on time"}]
assert [t["id"] for t in by_status(same)] == [4, 9], "tickets with the same status come out in id order"
queue = [{"id": 2, "status": "on time"}, {"id": 1, "status": "breached"}]
by_status(queue)
assert [t["id"] for t in queue] == [2, 1], "leaves the caller's list in its order"

tasks.title: Classes and objects
tasks.idea: The reader writes a class Agent: Agent(name) stores name and starts an empty list of ticket ids, take(ticket_id) adds one, load() returns how many the agent holds, and repr(agent) is text such as Agent('lee', 2).
checks: load() returns the number of tickets taken, which fails a method that prints the count.
Two agents keep separate ticket lists, which fails a list made once in the class body.
repr() gives the name and load in the form Agent('lee', 2), which fails a class with no __repr__.
tasks.q: Write a class Agent. Agent(name) makes an agent with that name and no tickets yet, and every agent keeps its own tickets. take(ticket_id) gives the agent one more ticket id, and load() returns how many ticket ids the agent holds. repr() of an agent named lee who holds two tickets is Agent('lee', 2).
tasks.tests:
lee = Agent("lee")
lee.take(101)
lee.take(102)
dana = Agent("dana")
dana.take(103)
assert lee.load() == 2, "load() returns how many tickets the agent took"
assert dana.load() == 1, "each agent keeps its own tickets"
assert repr(lee) == "Agent('lee', 2)", "repr() shows the name and the load"

tasks.title: Inheritance
tasks.idea: The starter holds a small Ticket(ticket_id, title) whose label() returns "#101 VPN down". The reader writes SecurityTicket(Ticket) whose __init__ also takes cve and whose label() returns the parent's label with "[security] " in front, so the result is "[security] #101 VPN down".
checks: A SecurityTicket is a Ticket for isinstance().
The title set by the parent's __init__ is there, which fails a subclass __init__ that skips super().__init__.
label() returns the parent's label with the prefix, which fails an override that drops the parent's text.
The cve is stored on the instance.
tasks.q: The starter holds a small Ticket class. Write SecurityTicket, a subclass of Ticket. SecurityTicket(ticket_id, title, cve) sets up everything a Ticket has and also keeps the cve argument as the attribute cve. Its label() returns the parent's label with "[security] " in front, so SecurityTicket(101, "VPN down", "CVE-2026-1234").label() returns "[security] #101 VPN down".
tasks.tests:
s = SecurityTicket(101, "VPN down", "CVE-2026-1234")
assert isinstance(s, Ticket), "a SecurityTicket is a Ticket"
assert s.title == "VPN down", "the parent's __init__ still sets the title"
assert s.label() == "[security] #101 VPN down", "label() puts [security] in front of the parent's label"
assert s.cve == "CVE-2026-1234", "keeps the cve on the ticket"

tasks.title: Iterators
tasks.idea: The reader writes first_and_rest(titles), which takes any iterable of titles that is not empty and returns a tuple of the first title and a list of the rest, using iter() and next(). first_and_rest(["Login page returns 500", "Printer jams"]) returns ("Login page returns 500", ["Printer jams"]).
checks: A list gives the first title and the rest.
The rest leaves out the first title, which fails a body that calls iter() on the list a second time.
An iterator passed in works too, which fails titles[0] and titles[1:].
tasks.q: Write first_and_rest(titles). titles is a list of ticket titles, or an iterator over them, with at least one title in it. Return a tuple of the first title and a list of the titles after it: first_and_rest(["Login page returns 500", "Printer jams"]) returns ("Login page returns 500", ["Printer jams"]). An iterator can be read only once and cannot be indexed, so reach for iter() and next().
tasks.tests:
result = first_and_rest(["Login page returns 500", "Printer jams", "VPN down"])
assert isinstance(result, tuple) and result[0] == "Login page returns 500", "returns a tuple that starts with the first title"
assert result[1] == ["Printer jams", "VPN down"], "the rest leaves out the first title"
assert first_and_rest(iter(["Printer jams", "VPN down"])) == ("Printer jams", ["VPN down"]), "works on an iterator too"

tasks.title: Scope
tasks.idea: The reader writes make_id_counter(start), which returns a function that hands out start, then start + 1, and so on, one id per call. With take = make_id_counter(100), three calls return 100, 101 and 102.
checks: Successive calls return start, start + 1 and start + 2, which fails an inner function without nonlocal (UnboundLocalError).
Two counters made separately count on their own, which fails a counter kept in a global.
tasks.q: Write make_id_counter(start). It returns a function that takes no arguments and hands out one id per call: start on the first call, then start + 1, and so on. With take = make_id_counter(100), three calls to take() return 100, 101 and 102. Two counters made by separate calls count on their own.
tasks.tests:
take = make_id_counter(100)
assert [take(), take(), take()] == [100, 101, 102], "successive calls hand out 100, 101 and 102"
a = make_id_counter(1)
b = make_id_counter(50)
a()
assert [a(), b()] == [2, 50], "two counters count on their own"
